text: Sourdough fermentation depends on a stable community of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria. The starter is maintained by discarding a portion of the culture and refreshing it with flour and water at regular intervals, which keeps the population in an exponential growth phase. Hydration is expressed as a baker's percentage relative to flour weight, and a wetter starter ferments faster because diffusion of nutrients through the matrix is less restricted. Temperature is the dominant variable: below eighteen degrees the bacteria outpace the yeast and the culture turns sour without rising. A mature starter doubles within four to six hours of feeding at room temperature.

Espresso extraction is governed by the interaction of grind size, dose, and pressure. Water at approximately ninety-three degrees is forced through a compacted bed of coffee at nine bars. Finer grinds increase surface area and resistance, extending contact time; coarser grinds allow channelling, where water finds a path of least resistance and leaves much of the bed under-extracted. Ratio is conventionally expressed as the mass of liquid out divided by the mass of dry coffee in. A typical shot uses eighteen grams of coffee to yield thirty-six grams of liquid in about twenty-five to thirty seconds.

The tempering of chocolate is a controlled crystallisation. Cocoa butter can solidify into six polymorphic forms, only one of which produces the desired snap and gloss. The chocolate is melted, cooled while agitated to seed the correct crystal form, then gently rewarmed to melt the unstable forms without destroying the seeds. Insufficient tempering produces bloom, a dull grey surface where fat has migrated and recrystallised. Dark chocolate is worked to about thirty-one degrees, milk and white chocolate a degree or two lower because their milk fats soften the crystal lattice. A properly tempered bar contracts slightly as it sets, which is what lets it release cleanly from a mould.

Stock is an extraction of collagen and aromatic compounds into water. Bones are simmered rather than boiled, because agitation emulsifies fat into the liquid and clouds it. Collagen converts to gelatin over several hours, which is what gives a finished stock body when chilled. Aromatics are added late, since their volatile compounds are driven off by prolonged heat. A white stock uses raw bones and is kept below a simmer for clarity; a brown stock roasts the bones first, which drives Maillard browning and gives colour and depth. Skimming early removes coagulated proteins before they can be stirred back in.

Bread staling is not primarily loss of moisture but retrogradation: the recrystallisation of gelatinised starch as it cools. This is why a stale loaf can be partly refreshed by heating, which re-melts the crystals, and why refrigeration accelerates staling while freezing arrests it. Crumb structure depends on gluten development, which aligns protein strands into an elastic network capable of retaining fermentation gases. Enriched doughs, which carry butter, eggs or milk, stale more slowly because fat interferes with starch recrystallisation and coats the gluten strands. A lean loaf is best eaten within a day, while a brioche keeps its crumb for several.
